use: The simplest way to buy or order: point at the thing at a counter, stall or menu.

example.ja: これとこれ、ください。
example.english: This and this, please.

notes: Add a count: kore futatsu kudasai (two of these).

use: Tells staff the item is a present so they wrap it; they often ask gojitaku you desu ka? (is it for yourself?) first.

example.romaji: purezento you desu. tsutsunde moraemasu ka?
example.ja: プレゼント用です。包んでもらえますか？
example.english: It's a present. Could you wrap it?

use: Ask before ordering or at the till; small places may be cash only.

example.ja: すみません、カード使えますか？
example.english: Excuse me, do you take cards?

notes: Genkin dake desu means cash only.

kana: ちょっとかんがえます
use: Polite way to leave without buying or to end a sales pitch; it usually means no.

example.ja: そうですね…ちょっと考えます。
example.english: Hmm... I'll think about it.

src: カードでお願いします
ja: カードでお願いします
kana: カードでおねがいします
use: Answer at the till when staff ask how you'll pay (oshiharai wa?).

example.ja: あ、カードでお願いします。
example.english: Oh, by card, please.

notes: Cash is genkin de. If staff ask ikkai barai de yoroshii desu ka (one payment?), just say hai.

kana: ふくろはだいじょうぶです
use: Answer when the cashier asks if you want a bag; daijoubu here means no thanks.

example.ja: あ、袋は大丈夫です。
example.english: Oh, I don't need a bag.

notes: Bags cost a few yen, so you'll be asked at most tills.

kana: ふくろおねがいします
use: Asks for a bag at the till; it usually costs a few yen.

example.romaji: fukuro onegai shimasu. hitotsu de ii desu.
example.ja: 袋お願いします。一つでいいです。
example.english: A bag, please. Just one is fine.

src: 試着してもいいですか
ja: 試着してもいいですか
kana: しちゃくしてもいいですか
romaji: shichaku shite mo ii desu ka
use: Ask a clothes-shop assistant before taking things to the fitting room (shichakushitsu).

example.romaji: sumimasen, kore shichaku shite mo ii desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、これ試着してもいいですか？
example.english: Excuse me, can I try this on?

notes: Staff usually answer douzo, kochira e (sure, this way).

src: レシートは大丈夫です
ja: レシートは大丈夫です
kana: レシートはだいじょうぶです
use: Said when the cashier hands over or offers the receipt.

example.romaji: reshiito wa daijoubu desu. arigatou gozaimasu.
example.ja: レシートは大丈夫です。ありがとうございます。
example.english: I don't need the receipt. Thank you.

notes: A formal receipt for expenses is a ryoushuusho.

use: Checks a price tag or quote; prices are shown either with tax (zeikomi) or without (zeinuki).

example.ja: この値段、税込みですか？
example.english: Does this price include tax?

use: Tells staff you don't need a bag, wrapping or a box; also works for anything you'd leave unchanged.

example.romaji: sugu tsukau node, kono mama de ii desu.
example.ja: すぐ使うので、このままでいいです。
example.english: I'll use it right away, so it's fine as it is.

notes: Kono mama means like this, unchanged.

use: Ends your order at a restaurant or counter; staff and speakers also use it to end a talk or report.

example.romaji: biiru futatsu to edamame, ijou desu.
example.ja: ビール二つと枝豆、以上です。
example.english: Two beers and edamame. That's all.

notes: Staff may check with ijou de yoroshii desu ka? (will that be all?).

use: Everyday way to say you're hungry; Japanese says it in the past form.

example.ja: あー、お腹すいた。何か食べよう。
example.english: Ugh, I'm starving. Let's eat something.

notes: Ask others with onaka suiteru? (are you hungry?). Men may say hara hetta.

use: Orders or offers another glass or bowl; add kudasai to staff.

example.ja: もう一杯飲もうよ。
example.english: Let's have one more.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、ビールもう一杯ください。

notes: Ippai on its own also means full or lots; the mou tells you it's one more.

use: Said when food arrives or you see it, before eating; after eating say oishii or oishikatta.

example.ja: うわ、おいしそう！いただきます。
example.english: Wow, that looks so good! Let's eat.

notes: -sou on any adjective means looks: takasou (looks expensive).

use: Said after finishing a meal; to a host or staff, follow with gochisousama deshita.

example.ja: あー、おいしかった。ごちそうさま！
example.english: Mm, that was delicious. Thanks for the meal!

examplePolite.ja: とてもおいしかったです。ごちそうさまでした。
examplePolite.english: That was really delicious. Thank you for the meal.

use: Asks for another bowl of rice or a refill, or offers one (okawari wa?).

example.ja: おかわりあるよ。いる？
example.english: There's seconds. Want some?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, gohan no okawari onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ご飯のおかわりお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could I get more rice?

notes: Okawari jiyuu means free refills. As a verb: okawari suru.

english: want to go for a drink?
use: Invites a friend or coworker out drinking; the negative question makes it easy to say no.

example.ja: 仕事終わったら、飲みに行かない？
example.english: Want to go for a drink after work?

examplePolite.ja: 今度、飲みに行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to go for a drink sometime?

notes: A nomikai is an organised drinking party with work or a club.

use: Offers to pay for a friend's food or drinks; they usually answer ii no? before accepting.

example.romaji: kyou wa watashi ga ogoru yo.
example.ja: 今日は私がおごるよ。
example.english: Today's on me.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa watashi ga gochisou shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は私がごちそうします。

notes: The treat itself is ogori; ogotte means treat me.

use: Groaned the night of or the morning after.

example.ja: 昨日飲み過ぎた…頭痛い。
example.english: I drank too much last night... my head hurts.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日はちょっと飲み過ぎました。
examplePolite.english: I had a bit too much to drink yesterday.

notes: -sugita works on any verb: tabesugita (ate too much). A hangover is futsukayoi.
